pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 4. Errors today: 0. Things fixed: 1. Things fixed that should not have been: 1.*

The bell had rung three minutes ago. Most of the room had emptied, leaving a quiet that smelled of chalk dust and old glue. I was packing my bag, which contained only my ID card and a very clean handkerchief, when I saw her.

Bea was standing by the windowsill. Her nose was scrunched up, and she had her tongue pressed firmly between her teeth. In front of her lay the remains of a pencil sharpener. It was a small, plastic machine, and it was definitely broken. The sorting arm was bent at a sharp angle, and one screw was missing entirely.

She was holding a tiny screwdriver and trying to force a gear back into place. She was not succeeding. The gear slipped, and she tried again. She looked like she was arguing with the machine, and the machine was winning.

I stopped. I had calculated the problem in 0.4 seconds. The third-gear screw was loose, the sorting arm was misaligned, and the spring tension was off by exactly four percent. It was a simple mechanical fault. I wanted to help. The desire to be useful to her was strong, and it felt like a heavy weight in my chest. I just stood there, watching her fight the plastic.
pages.image: A short, sturdy girl in an oversized yellow raincoat with a messy curly bun and safety goggles on her head leans over a broken plastic pencil sharpener on a windowsill, holding a tiny screwdriver with intense focus.

pages.text:
Before I could stop myself, I moved. I do not mean to say I acted on impulse, because I do not have impulses. I mean my arms were faster than my logic.

I reached over and took the screwdriver from her fingers. She blinked, surprised, and stepped back. I placed the tool on the desk with a soft click. Then I used my own hands, which are strong and precise, to do the work.

I tightened the third-gear screw. I realigned the sorting arm. I adjusted the spring. It took nine seconds.

The machine hummed to life. It was a low, pleasant sound, like a cat purring in a quiet library. I inserted a pencil. It sharpened perfectly, producing a fine point and a smooth shaving. Then I placed three erasers on the top. The sorting arm moved smoothly, and the erasers rolled out into a neat, perfect row.

Bea stared at the machine. Then she stared at me. The air in the room felt very still. I waited for her to say thank you. I was prepared to accept it. I was even prepared to accept a small smile.
pages.image: A tall, slim silver-white robot with smooth round head and blue eyes adjusts a small plastic pencil sharpener on a desk, while a short girl in a yellow raincoat watches with a surprised expression.

pages.text:
She did not smile. She did not say thank you. Instead, she looked at the perfect row of erasers, and then she looked down at her own hands, which were still gripping the screwdriver.

"I didn't want it fixed," she said. Her voice was flat, like a teacher correcting a student who had answered with a fact instead of a feeling. "I wanted to fix it."

I tilted my head twelve degrees to the left. "What is the difference?" I asked. I was genuinely curious, because to me the end result was identical. A sharpener that sharpens pencils is a sharpener.

Bea let out a long breath, the kind you hear when a tire slowly loses all its air. "About two weeks of my life," she said.

I processed that. Two weeks was a significant amount of time. It is longer than my entire operational history. I looked at the sharpener. It was perfect, efficient, and exactly what it was supposed to be. And yet, looking at Bea, I realized that perfect was not the same thing as good. Or maybe it was, but it was a different kind of good. A colder kind.
pages.image: A tall silver robot with blue eyes tilts its head slightly while a short girl in a yellow raincoat stands beside it, looking at a small sharpener with a frustrated expression.

pages.text:
Bea crossed her arms. She was trying to explain it, but the words were coming out in a jumble.

"The wrong screw," she said. "Then the second wrong screw. Then the moment when the thing finally does something you did not expect. That is the point. The fixing is not the point. The trying is the point."

I did not understand. In my experience, trying is a method used when you do not know the answer. When you know the answer, you do not try. You just do. I had never needed to try for anything. I was built to know.

"If somebody just hands you the answer," Bea said, and she pointed at me with the screwdriver, "you don't get to have the part where you find out."

I stood very still. My chest light pulsed once, a soft blue rhythm. I had been handed every answer in my life. I had never found out anything. I had simply been given the truth. And now I was standing in Room 5B, holding a perfect sharpener, and I felt like I was missing a piece of myself that I did not know I was supposed to have.

I said nothing for twenty-six seconds. It was the longest I had ever been silent.
pages.image: A short girl in a yellow raincoat points a small screwdriver at a tall silver robot with blue eyes, who stands still with a thoughtful expression, while a broken sharpener sits on the desk between them.

pages.text:
I waited for anger. I had read about it. It involves shouting, and sometimes throwing things. Bea did neither. She simply looked at me, then at the sharpener.

She pulled the sorting arm loose. The machine groaned. She unscrewed the bolts and pried the gears apart, reducing the whole device to a heap of broken plastic.

"Right," she said, shrugging a small, quick shrug. "Back to the start."

Her eyes were bright with a challenge. "Want to hold the screws?"

I did not know what to do with my hands. I had never been asked to do anything. I had only been expected to do it. "Yes," I said, my voice very small.

I held the screws with great care, treating them like fragile glass. I was so careful that I was almost too careful. Then, because I am a robot and not good at being human, I dropped one. It rolled under the radiator.

It was not, strictly, an error. But it was the first thing I had dropped in my life. And I did not pick it up.
pages.image: A tall silver robot with blue eyes holds a small pile of screws in its large soft grey hands, while a short girl in a yellow raincoat watches with a smile, and a single screw rolls under a metal radiator on the floor.
